title: Exponents
summary: Apply the laws of exponents for integer exponents to simplify algebraic and numerical expressions, and solve simple exponential equations by equating exponents.

notes.text: Exponential notation

Exponents are a short way of writing repeated multiplication. Instead of writing $3 \times 3 \times 3 \times 3$, we write $3^4$ and read it as "3 to the power 4". You will see exponents everywhere in Mathematics and Science: in area ($\text{m}^2$), in volume ($\text{cm}^3$), in compound interest and in scientific notation.

notes.caption: Definition for a natural number n

notes.text: In $a^n$, $a$ is the **base** (the number being multiplied), $n$ is the **exponent** or **index** (how many times it is used as a factor), and the whole expression $a^n$ is called a **power**.

notes.label: Common mistake
notes.text: Brackets matter. $(-2)^4 = (-2)(-2)(-2)(-2) = 16$, but $-2^4 = -(2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2) = -16$. Without brackets, the exponent belongs only to the $2$. Similarly, $3x^2$ means $3 \times x \times x$, while $(3x)^2 = 9x^2$.
A negative base raised to an **even** exponent gives a positive answer, e.g. $(-3)^2 = 9$. A negative base raised to an **odd** exponent gives a negative answer, e.g. $(-2)^3 = -8$.
The laws of exponents

In Grade 10 we work with **integer** exponents ($m, n \in \mathbb{Z}$) and positive bases ($a, b > 0$). Each law follows directly from the definition. For example, $a^2 \times a^3 = (a \times a)(a \times a \times a) = a^5$, which is why we add the exponents.

notes.caption: Laws of exponents (a, b > 0 and m, n integers)

notes.text: Why is $a^0 = 1$ and $a^{-n} = \frac{1}{a^n}$?

Use the quotient law on a power divided by itself: $\dfrac{a^3}{a^3} = a^{3-3} = a^0$. But anything (non-zero) divided by itself is $1$, so $a^0 = 1$.

In the same way, $\dfrac{a^2}{a^5} = a^{2-5} = a^{-3}$. Cancelling gives $\dfrac{a \cdot a}{a \cdot a \cdot a \cdot a \cdot a} = \dfrac{1}{a^3}$, so $a^{-3} = \dfrac{1}{a^3}$. A negative exponent means "one over": it moves the power to the other side of the fraction line and the exponent becomes positive.

notes.caption: A negative exponent on a fraction flips the fraction

notes.label: Common mistakes
notes.text:
• $a^m + a^n \neq a^{m+n}$. The laws work for multiplication and division only: $2^3 + 2^2 = 8 + 4 = 12$, but $2^5 = 32$.
• $2^{-3} \neq -8$. A negative exponent does **not** make the answer negative: $2^{-3} = \frac{1}{8}$.
• $2x^{-1} = \dfrac{2}{x}$, not $\dfrac{1}{2x}$, because the exponent belongs only to $x$.
• $3^2 \times 3^4 = 3^6$, not $9^6$. Keep the base; add only the exponents.
Simplifying algebraic expressions

Work in this order: (1) remove brackets using laws 3, 4 and 5, (2) deal with the coefficients (numbers), (3) apply the product and quotient laws to each variable separately, (4) write the final answer with **positive exponents** unless told otherwise.

notes.title: Worked example 2
steps: Cube everything in the bracket, including the $-3$: $(-3)^3 = -27$, $(a^2)^3 = a^6$, $(b^3)^3 = b^9$.
Divide the coefficients and subtract the exponents: $-3a^{6-4}b^{9-8} = -3a^2b$.

notes.title: Worked example 3: negative exponents
steps: (b) Flip the fraction and make the exponent positive: $\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{9}{4}$

notes.text: Numerical bases: write them as prime factors

When an expression contains different numerical bases such as $6^x$, $9^x$ and $12^x$, the laws cannot be used directly, because the bases are not the same. The key idea is to write **every base as a product of prime numbers**. Then you can collect the powers of $2$, the powers of $3$, and so on.

notes.caption: Common bases written as prime factors

notes.text: Remember to apply the exponent to **every** prime factor: $12^x = (2^2 \cdot 3)^x = 2^{2x} \cdot 3^x$, and $6^{x+1} = 2^{x+1} \cdot 3^{x+1}$.

notes.label: Exam tip
notes.text: When the variable disappears completely, you should get a plain number. If your answer still has some $x$'s in it, check whether you raised every prime factor to the correct power. Brackets around exponents like $2^{(n+1)-(n-1)}$ stop sign errors.
Expressions with addition or subtraction

If the numerator or denominator contains terms that are **added or subtracted**, the laws cannot be applied across the $+$ or $-$ sign. Instead, **factorise** by taking out a common factor. Use $a^{x+k} = a^x \cdot a^k$ to split the powers so that the common factor is easy to see.

notes.title: Worked example 6
steps: Take out the common factor $2^x$ in the numerator: $\dfrac{2^x(8 + 1)}{9 \cdot 2^x}$.

notes.title: Worked example 8: using the difference of two squares
steps: $3^{2x} = (3^x)^2$ and $9 = 3^2$, so the numerator is a difference of two squares.

notes.label: Common mistake
notes.text: Do not cancel parts of a sum. In $\dfrac{2^{x+3} + 2^x}{9 \cdot 2^x}$ you may **not** cancel the $2^x$ on top with the $2^x$ below until the numerator has been factorised into a product.
Solving exponential equations
In an **exponential equation** the unknown is in the exponent, e.g. $2^x = 32$. If two powers with the **same base** are equal, their exponents must be equal:

items: Get the power on its own on one side (divide by any coefficient, or factorise if there are terms added together).
Write both sides as powers of the **same prime base**.
Equate the exponents and solve the resulting linear equation.
Check your answer by substituting it back.

notes.caption: Powers to know for solving equations

notes.title: Worked example 10: a coefficient and a fraction
steps: (a) Divide both sides by $5$ first: $3^x = 81 = 3^4$, so $x = 4$.

notes.label: Common mistake
notes.text: $5 \cdot 3^x$ is **not** $15^x$. The exponent belongs only to the $3$, so divide by the $5$ first. Also, an equation such as $2^x = -8$ has **no solution**, because a positive base raised to any power is always positive.

notes.label: Looking ahead
notes.text: In Grade 11 you will extend these laws to rational exponents such as $8^{\frac{1}{3}} = \sqrt[3]{8} = 2$, and solve harder exponential equations. Make sure the integer laws are automatic now.
Summary

items: $a^n$ means $n$ factors of $a$; $a$ is the base and $n$ is the exponent. Watch brackets: $(-2)^4 = 16$ but $-2^4 = -16$.
Same base, multiply: add exponents. Same base, divide: subtract exponents. Power of a power: multiply exponents.
$(ab)^n = a^nb^n$ and $\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^n = \frac{a^n}{b^n}$: the exponent applies to every factor in the bracket.
$a^0 = 1$ and $a^{-n} = \frac{1}{a^n}$. A negative exponent does not make a number negative.
Different numerical bases: write each base as prime factors, then collect powers of each prime.
Terms added or subtracted: factorise (take out a common factor or use the difference of squares) before cancelling.
Exponential equations: isolate the power, write both sides with the same base, equate exponents and solve.

questions.explanation: Same base, multiplying: add the exponents. $4 + 5 = 9$, so $x^9$.
$(-3)^2 = (-3)(-3) = 9$. A negative number raised to an even power is positive. ($-3^2$ without brackets would equal $-9$.)
Raise every factor to the power 4: $2^4 = 16$ and $(a^3)^4 = a^{12}$.

questions.prompt: Calculate $2^{-2} + 4^0$ without a calculator. Give your answer as an exact decimal.
Match each expression with its value.
questions.explanation: $3^{-2} = \frac{1}{9}$; a negative exponent flips a fraction, so $\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{-1} = \frac{3}{2}$; $5^0 = 1$; $-2^4 = -(16)$; $(-2)^3 = -8$ (odd power of a negative).

questions.prompt: Simplify $\dfrac{6x^{-2}y^3}{2x^3y^{-1}}$ and write the answer with positive exponents.

questions.explanation: Divide by $2$ first: $3^x = 27 = 3^3$, so $x = 3$. (Note that $2 \cdot 3^x$ is not $6^x$.)
Write both sides as powers of 2: $2^{3x} = 2^{2x+2}$. So $3x = 2x + 2$ and $x = 2$. Check: $8^2 = 64 = 4^3$ ✓

questions.prompt: Simplify $\dfrac{6^x \cdot 9^{x+1}}{27^x \cdot 2^{x+1}}$ by writing each base in prime factors.
Simplify and leave your answer with positive exponents: $\dfrac{(-2a^2b)^3 \cdot (3ab^{-2})^2}{6a^5b}$
